name: watermark-pattern
context: Events arrive out of order, so an operator cannot tell when it is safe to close a window. The watermark pattern carries a progress marker through the stream: a watermark at time t declares that no further element with a timestamp at or before t is expected. Watermarks are generated at or immediately after sources, flow with the data, advance each operator's event-time clock, and are re-emitted downstream as that operator's clock advances. An operator with several inputs takes the minimum of its inputs' watermarks.
benefits: Gives a deterministic basis for window closure under out-of-order data, independent of arrival jitter
Bounds correctness loss explicitly: the tolerated lateness is a declared number rather than an accident of network timing
Propagates through the whole topology, so every downstream stage agrees on the current event time
Enables reprocessing of history fast: a job can fast-forward weeks of event time with seconds of processing
Works with late data instead of for it — records inside the bound correct results rather than being dropped
tradeoffs: Waiting for out-of-orderness adds latency to every windowed result — the lateness bound is paid in wall-clock time
An operator combining several inputs is only as advanced as its slowest input, so one idle partition stalls the pipeline
An over-aggressive watermark silently drops data; there is no error, only missing records
Watermarks must be monotonic and cannot be corrected after emission
Each operator maintains its own event-time clock, so debugging 'why did this window close early' means reasoning across several of them
use_cases: Event-time windows over a stream where records can arrive minutes out of order
Late-data handling with a declared grace or allowed-lateness bound
Detecting an idle partition or a silent upstream so window firing does not stall
Aligning multiple input streams so a join sees a consistent event-time frontier on both sides
Replaying historical data into a live pipeline where event time must advance far faster than wall clock
avoid_when: The input is strictly ordered by event time and produced by a single trusted source
The computation is stateless — no window, no timer, nothing that needs to know time has passed
Processing-time semantics are acceptable and the simpler wall clock will do
The lateness bound cannot be estimated, which makes any watermark choice arbitrary
component_types: Watermark generator: attaches or produces a timestamp marker at the source, bounded-out-of-orderness or generator-based
Watermark propagation: marker travels with records through the topology
Event-time clock: per-operator current event time, advanced when a watermark arrives
Watermark minimiser: for multi-input operators, the minimum across inputs
Idleness detector: marks an idle input so it stops holding the frontier back
Window trigger and grace: uses the advanced clock to fire windows and bound late arrivals
anti_patterns: Failing to mark idle sources, so one silent partition freezes window firing across the whole job
Generating watermarks from wall-clock time while using event-time windows, which converts network jitter into dropped data
Setting an unbounded lateness bound and holding partial state indefinitely
Assuming a watermark means results are final — results can still be corrected inside the lateness bound
Comparing timestamps from different input streams that have never been aligned on a common frontier
best_practices: Bound out-of-orderness from a measured distribution of event-time to arrival-time delay, not from a guess
Mark idle inputs explicitly rather than waiting for a timeout to unblock the pipeline
Expose the current watermark per operator as a metric — a stalled watermark is the first symptom of a stalled pipeline
Keep the lateness bound and the grace period consistent with each other and with the retention policy
Log dropped-late-record counts; a silent drop is the characteristic failure of this pattern
design_principles: Watermarks are generated at the source and nowhere else — downstream operators only re-emit what they received
The frontier of a multi-input operator is the minimum over its inputs, never the average
Idleness is information: an input that stopped must be marked so it stops holding the frontier back
The lateness bound is declared, not discovered — a watermark without a bound is a guess
Watermarks are monotonic; a mistake is corrected downstream, never by rewinding the marker
references: Apache Flink, Timely Stream Processing — Watermarks in parallel streams and the minimum-over-inputs rule, https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-master/docs/concepts/time/
Apache Kafka, Configuring a Streams Application — max.task.idle.ms and related idle-handling settings, https://kafka.apache.org/43/streams/developer-guide/config-streams/
Apache Kafka, Core Concepts — grace period, window close and out-of-order handling, https://kafka.apache.org/43/streams/core-concepts/
